The one that can exhibit highest paramagnetic
behaviour among the following is :

gly = glycinato; bpy = 2, 2'-bipyridine
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
(A) $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{2+}$ is $3d^{6}$; with the strong-field nitrogen donors bpy, en and $\mathrm{NH}{}_{3}$ it is low spin, $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$, with no unpaired electron.

(B) $\mathrm{Pd}{}^{2+}$ is $4d^{8}$ and square planar, with no unpaired electron.

(C) For cobalt, $x+2(-2)+2(-1)=-1$ gives $x=+5$, so $\mathrm{Co}{}^{5+}$ is $3d^{4}$; with $\Delta _{o}>P$ it is $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{0}$, with 2 unpaired electrons.

(D) $\mathrm{Ti}{}^{3+}$ is $3d^{1}$, with 1 unpaired electron.

The cobalt complex has the most unpaired electrons and is the most paramagnetic.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
The Crystal Field Stabilization Energy

(CFSE) of [CoF$_{3}(H_{2}O)_{3}$] ($\Delta_{0}$ < P) is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{Co}{}^{3+}$ is $3d^{6}$. Since $\Delta _{o}<P$, electrons enter $e_{g}$ before pairing in $t_{2g}$, giving the high-spin configuration $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}$ with 4 unpaired electrons.

$\text{CFSE}=(-0.4\times 4+0.6\times 2)\Delta _{o}=(-1.6+1.2)\Delta _{o}=-0.4\Delta _{o}$

The single electron pair of $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}$ is already present in the free $3d^{6}$ ion, so no extra pairing energy enters; a $P$ term arises only for pairs forced by the field, as in low-spin $t_{2g}^{6}$ ($-2.4\qquad \Delta _{o}+2P$).

Hence, the correct option is (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot

text:
If the equilibrium constant for
 A ⇌ B + C is $K_{eq}^{(1)}$ and that of

B + C ⇌ P is $K_{eq}^{(2)}$, the equilibrium

constant for A ⇌ P is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We have two reactions:

$A⇌B+C\text{with}K_{eq}^{(1)}$

$B+C⇌P\text{with}K_{eq}^{(2)}$

We want the equilibrium constant for the overall reaction

$A⇌P.$

How to combine the equilibrium constants
When two reactions are added to yield a net (overall) reaction, the equilibrium constant of the net reaction is the product of the equilibrium constants of the individual reactions. Formally:

$\text{(Reaction 1)}+\text{(Reaction 2)}\Rightarrow \text{(Net Reaction)},$

and

$K_{\text{net}}=K_{\text{(Reaction 1)}}\times K_{\text{(Reaction 2)}}.$

Applying it here

Reaction 1: $A\to B+C$ has $K_{eq}^{(1)}.$

Reaction 2: $B+C\to P$ has $K_{eq}^{(2)}.$

When we add them,

$A⏟_{\text{Reactant 1}}⟶B+C_{\text{Products of Reaction 1}=\text{Reactants of Reaction 2}}⟶P⏟_{\text{Product of Reaction 2}}.$

So the net reaction is $A\to P$, and its equilibrium constant is

$K_{eq}^{\text{(net)}}=K_{eq}^{(1)}\times K_{eq}^{(2)}.$

Thus, the correct answer is:

$K_{eq}^{(1)}\qquad K_{eq}^{(2)}.$

Hence, the answer (Option D) is correct.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot

text:
The reaction in which the hybridisation of the
underlined atom is affected is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the option in which the hybridisation of the underlined atom is affected, we need to look at each reaction and predict the changes in hybridisation that might be occurring with the reactants and products.

Option A:

In the reaction $Xe–F_{4}+SbF_{5}\to$, xenon tetrafluoride (XeF$_{4})$ reacts with antimony pentafluoride (SbF$_{5})$. XeF$_{4}$ is a square planar molecule, and the central Xe atom is $sp^{3}d^{2}$ hybridised. The reaction with SbF$_{5}$ can lead to the formation of a complex where the hybridisation of Xe changes if it coordinates with SbF$_{5}$. Thus, the hybridisation of Xe may indeed be affected in this case.

  
    $Xe–F_{4}$
    +
    SbF$_{5}$
    $\to$
    [XeF$_{3}$]$^{+}$[SbF$_{6}$]$^{-}$
  

  
    $sp^{3}d^{2}$
    
    
    
    $sp^{3}d$   $sp^{3}d^{2}$
  

Option B:

In the reaction $H_{2}S–O_{4}+NaCl⟶^{420K}$, sulfuric acid $(H_{2}SO_{4})$ reacts with sodium chloride (NaCl). The underlined atom here is sulfur (S). In sulfuric acid, sulfur is hybridised as $sp^{3}$. Upon heating, there is typically no change in the hybridisation of the sulfur atom within sulfuric acid as part of this reaction. Therefore, the hybridisation of S is likely not affected.

Option C:

In the reaction $H_{3}P–O_{2}⟶^{Disproportionation}$, hypophosphorous acid $(H_{3}PO_{2})$ is undergoing a disproportionation reaction. The underlined atom is phosphorus (P). In $H_{3}PO_{2}$, the hybridisation of the phosphorus atom is $sp^{3}$. A typical disproportionation reaction of hypophosphorous acid would result in phosphine $(PH_{3})$ and phosphorous acid $(H_{3}PO_{3})$. The phosphorus atom in $PH_{3}$ will have $sp^{3}$ hybridisation while in $H_{3}PO_{3}$ the phosphorus atom is $sp^{3}$ hybridised. Given this information, the hybridisation of phosphorus may or may not change, depending on the resulting state of the phosphorus atom in the products. It's not a clear-cut case without knowing the specific products.

Option D:

In the reaction $N–H_{3}⟶^{H^{+}}$, ammonia $(NH_{3})$ is reacting with a proton $(H^{+})$. The underlined atom is nitrogen (N). In $NH_{3}$, the nitrogen is $sp^{3}$ hybridised. When ammonia accepts a proton, it forms ammonium ion $(NH_{4}^{+})$, which is also $sp^{3}$ hybridised. Therefore, there is no change in the hybridisation of nitrogen in this case.

Given this information, the option in which the hybridisation of the underlined atom is most clearly affected is Option A, where the reaction can lead to coordination changes to the Xe atom, potentially affecting its hybridisation.

text:
The shortest wavelength of H atom in the
Lyman series is $λ_{1}$. The longest wavelength in
the Balmer series of He$^{+}$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For Shortest wavelength energy should be maximum.

For maximum energy transition must be from n = $\infty$ to n = 1.

$\frac{1}{λ_{1}}=R_{H}(1)^{2}\left [\frac{1}{1}-0\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{λ_{1}}=R_{H}$

For longest wavelength, $\Delta$E = minimum. 
For Balmer series n = 3 to n = 2 will have $\Delta$E minimum
for He$^{+}$,
 Z = 2

So $\frac{1}{λ_{2}}=R_{H}(2)^{2}\left [\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{λ_{2}}=R_{H}\times \frac{5}{9}$

$\Rightarrow$ $λ_{2}=λ_{1}\times \frac{9}{5}$

text:
The major product [C] of the following reaction
sequence will be :

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{NaBH}{}_{4}$ reduces only the aldehyde, $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CHO}\longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}{}_{2}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$, and $\mathrm{SOCl}{}_{2}$ converts the alcohol into allyl chloride [A], $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}$.

Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene with the allyl cation gives allylbenzene [B], $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}$.

$\mathrm{D}{}^{+}$ adds to the terminal $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}$ (Markovnikov addition), giving the secondary cation $\mathrm{C}_{6}\mathrm{H}_{5}\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{C}^{+}\mathrm{HCH}_{2}\mathrm{D}$.

A 1,2-hydride shift from the benzylic $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}$ converts it into the resonance-stabilised benzylic cation $\mathrm{C}_{6}\mathrm{H}_{5}\mathrm{C}^{+}\mathrm{HCH}_{2}\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{D}$.

Capture by $\mathrm{Br}{}^{-}$ gives [C], $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{Br})-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{D}$.

Hence, the correct option is (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot

text:
The molecule in which hybrid MOs involve only
one d-orbital of the central atom is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{XeF}{}_{4}$: Xe has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs, so it is $sp^{3}d^{2}$ hybridised (two d orbitals).

$[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{4}]{}^{2-}$: $\mathrm{Ni}{}^{2+}$ is $3d^{8}$; the strong-field $\mathrm{CN}{}^{-}$ ligands pair the electrons, leaving one 3d orbital empty, so it is $dsp^{2}$ hybridised (one d orbital, square planar).

$[\mathrm{CrF}{}_{6}]{}^{3-}$: $\mathrm{Cr}{}^{3+}$ is $3d^{3}$, which leaves two inner 3d orbitals empty, so it is $d^{2}sp^{3}$ hybridised (two d orbitals).

$\mathrm{BrF}{}_{5}$: Br has 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, so it is $sp^{3}d^{2}$ hybridised (two d orbitals).

Only $[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{4}]{}^{2-}$ uses a single d orbital.

Hence, the correct option is (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot

text:
A 100 mL solution was made by adding 1.43 g
of $Na_{2}CO_{3}.xH_{2}O$. The normality of the solution
is 0.1 N. The value of x is $_____$.

(The atomic mass of Na is 23 g/mol)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Molar mass of $Na_{2}CO_{3}.xH_{2}O$

= 23 × 2 + 12 + 48 + 18x

= 46 + 12 + 48 + 18x

= (106 + 18x)

As $n_{$factor} in dissolution will be determined from net cationic or anionic charge; which is 2

Eq wt = $\frac{M}{2}$ = (53 + 9x)

volume = 100 ml
= 0.1 Litre

Normality = 
     No. of equivalents of solute
     Volume of solution (in L)

$\Rightarrow$ 0.1= $\frac{\frac{1.43}{53+9x}}{0.1}$

$\Rightarrow$ 53 + 9x = 143

$\Rightarrow$ 9x = 90

$\Rightarrow$ x = 10

text:
The number of molecules with energy greater
than the threshold energy for a reaction
increases five fold by a rise of temperature
from $27^{o}C$ to $42^{o}C$. Its energy of activation in
J/mol is $_____$.

(Take ln 5 = 1.6094; R = 8.314 J mol$^{–1} K^{–1})$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\because$ k = A$e^{-\frac{Ea}{RT}}$

$T_{1} = 300K,  T_{2} = 315K$

As per question $K_{T2} = 5K_{T1}$ as molecules activated are increased five times so K will increase five times.

$\ln \left (\frac{K_{T2}}{K_{T1}}\right )$ = $\frac{E_{a}}{R}\left (\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ ln 5 = $\frac{E_{a}}{R}\left (\frac{15}{300\times 315}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $E_{a} =$ $\frac{1.6094\times 8.314\times 300\times 315}{15}$

= 84297.47 Joules/mole
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2020 (Online) 4th September Evening Slot
